But what then happens is, rather than seeing the order, grabbing the book from their warehouse, and shipping it, the online store sees the order, finds the listed press, and then places an order with them. This is why those books generally have a "Usually ships within 2-3 weeks" notation on them.

Amazon doesn't list everything with an ISBN, if memory serves. You need an ASIN as well (which is a special Amazon number), which means someone has to physically enter the book into Amazon's system to get one. A lot of vanity press books are listed on Amazon but not available through Amazon--they're only "Available through these sellers"--because a seller actually went and entered the book into Amazon on their sellers' page/through their Amazon storefront. Some vanity presses will do this for you--for an extra fee, of course--as part of a special "distribution package."

One final note (unless anyone has questions, which I am happy to answer as long as they don't out me): There's nothing wrong with legitimate self-publishing, at least not to an extent. I've self-published a few things myself--short stories related to my main series, generally--through Amazon, and made myself a nice little chunk of extra change on each one. (And by "nice little chunk" I mean the low five figures, which is nothing to sneeze at for a little 30k word side story.) Almost all of my writer friends have done the same. It's a nice secondary income stream, with the added benefit that it pays monthly instead of every six months the way commercial houses do (assuming you earn out your advance, which not every book/every writer does). It's also great for those who are reasonably good and extremely prolific, so can turn out a book a month, or something, or who want to try something different--I've had an idea for a while for an "installment novel," something like Maupin's Tales of the City (a series of columns that were collected into novels), to be released monthly. I just haven't gotten to it yet.

Point is, there's nothing wrong with self-publishing through Amazon, as long as you're/they're honest about it. But vanity presses are by and large NOT honest. They charge you for editing, cover design, layout, publishing, AND generally pay a royalty rate that's way lower even than commercial houses, much less what Amazon offers. They offer little to no distribution and make you pay for what they do offer. A lot of the time they make you buy dozens of copies of your own book, which you then have to try to sell on your own, which sucks. They lie to inexperienced (or, well, dumb) writers and tell them this is how publishing really works or this is how all writers started out, which is NOT true (a lot of the time they'll tell wildly inaccurate or misrepresented stories about John Grisham or Jackie Susann as evidence. Yes, John Grisham ended up selling copies of his own book out of his trunk, but it was published by a legitimate small press which went under, so he was selling the remaining copies, and if memory serves it was aimed at a specific audience which he had better access to than a bookseller would. Yes, Jackie Susann used to take donuts to truck drivers who stocked drugstores and airports with paperbacks, but distribution was done very differently back then and it was really more of a PR move than anything else, since her book was released on the NYT list--her publisher had already done the work to get her into enough stores to make that happen. But vanity presses never tell the truth about this).

By making you submit your book "for acceptance," they give the impression that there is actually a selection process and the book has to meet a certain quality standard to be accepted, which is NOT true. By offering "manuscript evaluation," they give you the impression that they actually know something about what makes a book good enough to be published, which, again, is NOT true.

Basically, they do nothing for you that you can't do yourself, and they charge you for it. They suck. But I'm glad your office fat got suckered by one...and next time she starts talking about it, you'll know the truth. :-)
